metadata.title: Herbert Markman and Positek, Inc. v. Westview Instruments, Inc. And Althon Enterprises, Inc, 517 U.S. 370 (1996) (No. 95-26)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Herbert Markman and Positek, Inc. v. Westview Instruments, Inc. And Althon Enterprises, Inc

Opinion filed: 1996-04-29

Docket No.: 95-26

Citations:
• 134 L. Ed. 2d 577
• 116 S. Ct. 1384
• 517 U.S. 370
• 1996 U.S. LEXIS 2804

Case holding summaries:
• “[T]he state of patent law in the common-law courts before 1800 led one historian to observe that ‘the reported cases are destitute of any decision of importance’ ” (quoting Hulme, On the Consideration of the Cite as: 561 U. S. (2010
• "We hold that the construction of a patent, including terms of art within its claim, is exclusively within the province of the court."
• "[A] patentee is free to be his own lexicographer. The caveat is that any special definition given to a word must be clearly defined in the specification."
• task of the court is to determine whether a definition fully comports with the specification and claims and will preserve the patent's internal coherence
• "[A]ny credibility determinations will be subsumed within the necessarily sophisticated analysis of the whole document, required by the standard construction rule that a term can be defined only in a way that comports with the instrument as a whole."
• "We accordingly think there is sufficient reason to treat construction of terms of art like many other responsibilities that we cede to a judge in the normal course of trial, notwithstanding its evidentiary underpinnings."
• noting that claim construction " 'falls somewhere between a pristine legal standard and a simple historical fact' "
• holding that “there is sufficient reason to treat construction of terms of art like many other responsibilities that we cede to a judge . . . .”
• applying the historical test in a patent infringement case
• In construing claims, the courts focus on “what one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention would have understood the term to mean.”
• discussing the importance of certainty in defining the scope of exclusive rights
• applying this test to determine that claim construction is best left to the judge
• explaining that willfulness may be found in cases in which opinions are incompetent, such as where an attorney does not examine necessary facts, or where the analysis is superficial
• holding that issue preclusion cannot be asserted against new defendants but noting that generally, stare decisis should promote uniformity in the claim construction of a given patent.
• holding extrinsic evidence may be used for the court's understanding of the patent
• “[A claim] term can be defined only in a way that comports with the instrument as a whole.”
• holding that claim construction is a matter of law for the court
• holding that claim construction is an issue of law for the court, not a question of fact for the jury.
• "Victory in an infringement suit requires a finding that the patent claim `covers the alleged infringer's product or process,' which in turn necessitates a determination of `what the words in the claim mean.'"
• "We hold that the construction of a patent, including terms of art within its claim, is exclusively within the province of the court."
• “If the action in question belongs in the law category, we then ask whether the particular trial decision must fall to the jury in order to preserve the substance of the common-law right as it existed in 1791.”
• “[D]etermining whether infringement occurred . . . is a question of fact, to be submitted to a jury.”
• "We hold that the construction of a patent, including terms of art within its claim, is exclusively within the province of the court."
• “Equally familiar is the descent of today’s patent infringement action from the infringement actions tried at law in the 18th century, and there is no dispute that infringement cases today must be tried to a jury, as their predecessors were more than two centuries ago.”
• "Victory in an infringement suit requires a finding that the patent claim `covers the alleged infringer's product or process,' which in turn necessitates a determination of `what the words in the claim mean.'"
• "[A claim] term can be defined only in a way that comports with the instrument as a whole."
• "Law clarification requires generalization, and some issues lend themselves to generalization much more than others."
• stating the “importance of uniformity in the treatment of a given patent” and “treating interpretive issues as purely legal will promote (though it will not guarantee) intrajurisdictional certainty”
• In construing claims, the courts focus on "what one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention would have understood the term to mean."
• calling the construction of a term of art following receipt of evidence a "mongrel practice"
• "So it turns out here, for judges, not juries, are the better suited to find the acquired meaning of patent terms."
• "[I]ssue preclusion could not be asserted against new and independent infringement defendants even within a given jurisdiction...."
• "notwithstanding [claim construction's] evidentiary underpinnings"
• holding that construing patent claims is a question of law for the judge, separate from determining whether infringement occurred which is a question of fact to be submitted to the jury
• holding that expert testimony must be evaluated in a manner that "fully comports with specification and the claims" and "preserve[s] the patent's internal coherence"
• explaining why judges "are the better suited to find the acquired meaning of patent terms"
• "We hold that the construction of a patent, including terms of art within its claim, is exclusively within the province of the court."
• noting his involvement in a patent case
• expressing concern regarding the ''uncertainty and the variety of conclusions which follows from an effort at purely historical accuracy''
• we must search the English common law for ''appropriate analogies'' rather than a ''precisely analogous common-law cause of action''
• holding that expert testimony must be evaluated in a manner that "fully comports with specification and the claims" and "preserve[s] the patent's internal coherence"
• classifying claim construction as "a mongrel practice" consisting of factual and legal components
• “[A]ny credi- 6 SOVERAIN SOFTWARE v. NEWEGG bility determinations will be subsumed within the neces- sarily sophisticated analysis of the whole document.”
• holding that the claims "must be read in view of the specification, of which they are a part"
• "We hold that the construction of a patent, including terms of art within its claim, is exclusively within the province of the court."
• “[T]he state of patent law in the common-law courts before 1800 led one historian to observe that ‘the reported cases are destitute of any decision of importance’ ” (quoting Hulme, On the Consideration of the Cite as: 561 U. S. (2010
• reasoning that allowing claim construction to be a question of law promotes both uniformity and certainty in the meaning of a patent's claims
• describing claim con- struction as an “interpretation” of claim terms
• "For claim construction purposes, the description may act as a sort of dictionary, which explains the invention and may define terms used in the claims."
• "[W]e see the importance of uniformity in the treatment of a given patent as an independent reason to allocate all issues of construction to the court."
